Meetings & Events Why does this exist? What am I exploring, creating, or teaching? If you had to describe MRL Glitch in one sentence, what would it be? What is the core artistic question we’re exploring? How do we transition from a physical body into a digital body? “Mirror as a portal” — is it a metaphor, a mechanic, or both? What must happen for it to feel like a portal? In 5 minutes, what should the visitor feel or realize Part of an experiment... What would be a conceptual failure? the team disagrees, fights amongst themselves What would be a conceptual success, even if the tech is simple? fully sinthetic moviment... I want to see if its worthy to work with MR What are the 3 keywords that should never be lost (tone + theme)? Solid, Liquid, Gas, Plasma in the digital world. What is the atom of the digital? Who is the audience (XR-familiar or general public)? Any accessibility considerations? How many people experience it at once (solo / small group / guided groups)? What is the entry ritual? How do people start (instruction, silence, guided intro, first “mirror moment”)? How much movement do you want from the visitor (walking, standing, seated)? Any “must-go” zones? Are there mandatory beats in the journey? (moment 1, moment 2, moment 3…) What are the space constraints we must respect (stairs, basement, wardrobe, narrow corridors, lighting, noise)? What is the safety rule that overrides everything? From these “digital body” dimensions — time, (de)form, size, gravity, multiplication, proximity, texture — which 2–3 are core, and which are optional? What exactly is the role of the glitch? controlled aesthetic effect? an error during translation? an emergent behavior from interaction? a narrative device? What are the limits of the digital body? (What can’t it do?) What are the rules of reality inside this world? (physics, scale, boundaries, identity) Do we want the visitor to feel in control… or feel translated/processed by a system? What is the most important moment where “physical → digital” becomes undeniable? What should be the primary interaction language: hand tracking, controllers, head/gaze, or something minimal/observational? Is space tracking / room anchoring required, or can the piece work without it? What must be rock-solid on Meta Quest 3 for the experience to work (hands, passthrough, anchors, video playback, audio, lighting)? What is the acceptable level of interactivity (high, medium, low) for the first public version? Do we need a Plan B mode if tracking fails on-site (fallback version, simplified loop, guided mode)? Who will operate the experience on-site (and how many people do we need)? What is the reset flow between groups? (restart app, recalibrate, clean headset, check batteries) What is the headset logistics plan? (number of devices, charging, spare devices, hygiene, storage) How do we handle calibration in the space (once per day / every group / as needed)? What is the visitor throughput goal (groups per hour, expected waiting time)? What are the failure scenarios we anticipate (tracking, app crash, overheating, lighting issues) and the quick response for each? What do we want to document (video of audience, logs, screenshots, notes), and who is responsible? mrl-glitch-fbx-import-to-unity.html.title: MRL Glitch - FBX import to Unity
mrl-glitch-fbx-import-to-unity.html.description:
Summary
Step by step: new Unity project (Quest 3) + import FBX/WAV
0) Pre-check (1 minute)
1) Create the project from scratch
2) Check if the FBX actually has animation
3) Create a clean test scene + play 1 FBX in the Editor
Helpfull Tutorial MRL Glitch FBX import to Unity Drawing 2025-12-17 18.29.47.excalidraw⚠ Switch to EXCALIDRAW VIEW in the MORE OPTIONS menu of this document. ⚠ You can decompress Drawing data with the command palette: 'Decompress current Excalidraw file'. For more info check in plugin settings under 'Saving' Confirm in Unity Hub that you have a Unity LTS installed (e.g.: 2022.3 LTS) with Android Build Support (SDK/NDK/OpenJDK). Quest 3 in Developer Mode and connected to MQDH (for Build & Run later). Open Unity Hub → New Project Template: 3D SRP. Suggested name: MRL_Glitch_FBX_Import Location: a dedicated folder just for this project (Documents/Unity/MetaQuest3). Create. Practical tip: as soon as the project opens, create a folder structure under Assets/ like this: Scenes FBX Audio Scripts For each FBX (01..., 02..., etc.): Click the FBX in the Project window. In the Inspector → Animation: Import Animations: ON Check if there is any clip listed (name of the take/clip). If no clip appears, this FBX may be just a “static mesh” (or the animation was exported into another file). Goal: confirm the imported FBX actually animates inside Unity (Editor) before going to Quest. Create a new scene (SRP) File → New Scene… Select Basic (URP) Click Create Save the scene File → Save As… Save to: Assets/Scenes/ Name: 00_SmokeTest_FBX.unity Drop one FBX into the scene In the Project window, open Assets/FBX/ Drag only 01_Razor_...Sequence.FBX into the Hierarchy (or directly into the Scene view) Try the simplest playback Press Play If the animation runs automatically → ✅ Step 3 done. If it does NOT animate automatically (common) → force playback with an Animator Create an Animator Controller: Project window → Right click → Create → Animation → Animator Controller Name: AC_SEQ01_Razor Select the FBX object in the Hierarchy Add Component → Animator Drag AC_SEQ01_Razor into the Animator Controller field Open the Animator window: Window → Animation → Animator In the Project window, expand the FBX (small triangle) to reveal its sub-assets Find the clip (often called Unreal Take) Drag the clip into the Animator graph (it becomes the default state) Press Play again → animation should run ✅ https://youtu.be/WxoeG3HQ0QE https://youtu.be/6RA9D2qEu9U?si=v_L-zQfNrGaFoVq7Why “if it doesn’t animate automatically” is quite common It’s very common to import an FBX that does contain an animation clip, drop the model into the scene, press Play… and see nothing moving. Unity often imports the clip as a sub-asset of the FBX, but does not automatically: create an Animator Controller, or assign that controller to the GameObject, or set the imported clip as the default state. So the animation exists, but nothing is telling Unity to play it. In those cases, you need to manually create an Animator Controller, assign it to the object, and add the imported clip as the default state in the Animator.

mrl-glitch-first-technical-setup.html.title: MRL Glitch - First Technical Setup
mrl-glitch-first-technical-setup.html.description:
Summary
Output of the Experiment
Configuration
Can I develop for Quest 3 on a Mac?
Architecture Diagram
1. User vs. Developer: two layers
2. What’s needed to develop with Unity on Mac (dev mode)
3. End-to-end flow for the first MR test https://youtu.be/0fQthzL9CP0Below is a compact “from user → developer” view for Meta Quest 3 + Unity on a MacAir 13 (M3, macOS Sequoia 15.7.1).Yes. Unity runs natively on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) via Unity Hub, and Meta officially supports Unity development for Quest on macOS (including Meta XR Simulator and Meta Quest Developer Hub on Mac). On Windows, many people use Quest Link to run content directly from the editor inside the headset. On macOS, the typical workflow is: Use Meta XR Simulator inside Unity for quick tests. Use Build & Run to deploy an Android build (APK) to the Quest 3 when you want to test on the real headset. MRL Glitch Architecture Diagram 2025-12-15 14.18.37.excalidraw⚠ Switch to EXCALIDRAW VIEW in the MORE OPTIONS menu of this document. ⚠ You can decompress Drawing data with the command palette: 'Decompress current Excalidraw file'. For more info check in plugin settings under 'Saving'Deployment USB-C Connection ADB Debugging Install to Quest Build Pipeline Unity Project Project Setup Tool Building Blocks Rig + Passthrough + Hands Android APK Build Development Environment Unity 2022.3 LTS Apple Silicon Android Build Support SDK + NDK OpenXR Plugin Meta XR SDK Developer Layer Meta Developer Account Organization Developer Mode ON Meta Quest Developer Hub User Layer Meta Account Meta Horizon App Guardian/Boundary Setup Hardware Meta Quest 3 Headset MacBook Air M3 iPhone/Android Phone Unity HUB Version 3.15.4 Unity 6.0 6000.0.61f1As a user (no development): You need: A Meta Quest 3 headset. A Phone (iOS or Android). The Meta Horizon on your phone (this is the companion app; In mid-2024, Meta renamed the old “Meta Quest” mobile app to “Meta Horizon” and changed the icon/UI.). A Meta account You sign into the Meta Horizon app on your phone with your Meta account. You pair the app with your Quest 3 (Settings → Devices → select headset). Basic flow: Turn on the headset → follow the initial setup (Wi-Fi, controllers, boundary/guardian, tutorial). Pair the headset with the mobile app (Menu → Devices → select your Quest; wait for “Connected”). During the very first setup of the Quest 3, the headset itself will also ask you to: either log in with an existing Meta account, or confirm / finish the login that started from the phone app. Use the headset as a normal consumer device: store apps, MR experiences, games, etc. As a developer (Unity + Quest 3): You are still a “normal user”, plus: A Meta Developer Account (same login, but with a developer organization created). To be a Quest / Horizon developer, your Meta account must be verified using one of two options: add a payment method (credit card, not PayPal), or set up two-factor authentication (2FA) via phone/SMS or authenticator app. Developer Mode enabled on the headset. Meta Quest Developer Hub (MQDH) installed on your Mac, logged in with the same Meta developer credentials as the headset. Unity with Android support on your Mac (2022.3.15f1+ or Unity 6.x LTS, with Android Build Support). Once those exist, you can build and deploy your own MR apps to the Quest.For Unity + Meta Quest 3 development on your Mac M3: Unity environment Install Unity Hub, then a Unity LTS version supported by Meta: Prefer Unity 2022.3 LTS (2022.3.15f1 or later) or Unity 6000.x LTS. Unity has two release families: Tech Stream – new features, less stable, changes quickly. LTS (Long Term Support) – production-focused: stability, bug and security fixes, long maintenance. When installing Unity via the Hub: Go to Installs → Install Editor → choose 2022.3.xxf1 LTS (Apple Silicon). Add Android Build Support (Android SDK, NDK, OpenJDK). Optionally add Mac Build Support (IL2CPP) if you also want native macOS builds. Developer account & organization Go to the Meta developer site and create a developer organization linked to your Meta account. Verify the account (credit/debit card or phone code). Developer Mode on the headset On your phone: open Meta Quest app → Menu → Devices → [your Quest] → Headset Settings → Developer Mode → toggle ON. Meta Quest Developer Hub (MQDH) on Mac Download and install MQDH for macOS from the official Meta developer site, or: Use Homebrew: brew install --cask meta-quest-developer-hub. Open MQDH and log in with your Meta developer credentials (same account as on the headset). Connect Quest 3 to MQDH Connect Quest 3 ⇆ Mac via USB-C. Put on the headset → accept USB debugging / file access prompts and select “Always allow from this computer”. In MQDH, open Device Manager and confirm the headset appears as Active (green). From MQDH you can see realtime device logs, install APKs via the Apps tab, and enable ADB over Wi-Fi for cable-free development. At this point you are “fully dev-enabled”: Unity can build Android apps, and MQDH + ADB let you install and debug them.Goal of this first prototype: Mixed Reality scene with passthrough + hand tracking + a static cube in space, no interaction yet. High-level steps (already accomplished, but good to document): Create Unity project for Quest New Unity 3D project. Set Build Target to Android. Install and enable XR Plug-in Management → OpenXR for Android. Install Meta XR SDK Import Meta XR Core / All-in-One SDK into the project. Run the Project Setup Tool to auto-configure player settings, OpenXR features, and recommended options for Meta Quest. Add XR “building blocks” Add the Camera Rig / Interactions Rig building block to the scene (this becomes your XR origin + tracking). Add the Passthrough building block → enables color passthrough so you see your real room with virtual content over it. Add the Real Hands building block → enables hand tracking visuals and basic input, using the same rig. Add a simple virtual object Create one Cube in the scene. Place it roughly at head height / slightly in front (initially fixed coords). No interaction logic yet (no grabbing, no physics beyond default). Build & Run to Quest 3 In Build Settings, add the open scene. Select your Quest as the Run Device (via USB). Click Build and Run → Unity builds an Android app and installs it on the headset. In the headset, find the app under Apps → Unknown Sources, or it auto-launches after install. Resulting experience (current state) You see your real environment via passthrough. A virtual cube floats in front of you (MR). Hand tracking is active (virtual hands visible), but: you don’t yet interact with the cube (no grab, no poke, no click); the cube is more like a spatial anchor / visual test. This is a good “Hello MR” baseline: color passthrough + hands + a simple object. Note: On macOS you can also use Meta XR Simulator to test your scene directly in the Unity Editor (simulated headset + hands) without building every time. For final validation on the real hardware, use Build & Run to deploy to the Quest 3.

mrl-glitch-general-context-of-the-tools..title: MRL Glitch - General Context of the Tools
mrl-glitch-general-context-of-the-tools..description:
Summary
General Context
1. Conceptual map: VR, AR, MR, XR, “extended reality”
2. Meta Quest 3 in 2025: position and highlights
3. Unity – history + strengths (for XR / creative tech)
4. Unreal Engine – history + strengths (for XR / creative tech)
5. Unity vs Unreal for Meta Quest 3 / MR, conceptually
Unity + Quest 3
Unreal + Quest 3
For a “creative technology” audience
What is the FBX format?
What to do with FBX in Unity? Virtual Reality (VR) Fully digital environment. The real world is blocked out; you see only a virtual scene. Tracking usually includes head + hands/controllers; sometimes full body. Typical use: games, simulations, training, narrative worlds. Augmented Reality (AR) You see the real world first. Digital elements are overlaid on top. Classic AR is “additive”: it doesn’t really understand or occlude the world, just draws on top (e.g., early phone AR, simple head-up displays). Mixed Reality (MR) Also shows the real world, but with spatial understanding: planes, depth, surfaces, sometimes hands and body; virtual objects can collide with tables, hide behind real objects, stick to walls, etc. Headsets like Meta Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro use color passthrough cameras + depth/mesh APIs to do this. XR / “Extended Reality” Umbrella term that covers VR + AR + MR and all hybrids. “Extended reality” is basically marketing-speak for “any reality with headsets / glasses in the mix”. So when someone says “extended reality”, they’re not contradicting “mixed reality”; they’re placing MR (and VR, AR) inside a larger conceptual bucket. Summary: XR = umbrella VR = fully virtual AR = real world + simple overlay MR = real world + spatially aware, interactive virtual layer Timeline & basics Lineage: Oculus → Meta Quest. Meta acquired Oculus in 2014; Quest 1 (2019), Quest 2 (2020), Quest 3 (2023). Quest 3 release: 10 October 2023. OS: Meta Horizon OS, a custom Android (currently based on Android 14). Hardware snapshot Standalone headset (no PC or console required), but can also connect to PC via Link / Air Link to run SteamVR etc. SoC: Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, roughly ~2× GPU performance vs Quest 2, with 8 GB RAM. Display: LCD, 2064×2208 px per eye, up to 120 Hz, pancake lenses → slimmer form factor and better clarity. Color passthrough cameras + depth sensor → supports room meshing, depth API, believable MR occlusion. Price & cost–benefit (2023–2025) Launch price: $499 (128 GB) and $649 (512 GB), marketed as “the world’s first mass-market mixed reality headset.” By 2024–2025: Meta introduced a cheaper Quest 3S (same chip, simpler optics) around $299. Meta is working on a future Quest 4 as a higher-end successor, expected around 2026. Even with price fluctuations, Quest 3 sits as the mid-range “reference” headset: much cheaper than Apple Vision Pro, more capable than older Quest 2 and most low-end mobile VR, fully standalone (unlike PS VR2, which requires a PS5). Position vs competitors (2025) Compared to Apple Vision Pro Vision Pro: ultra-high-end, eye tracking, micro-OLED displays, Mac integration, much higher price. Quest 3: lower resolution but still sharp, mass-market pricing, huge games catalog, more approachable for experimentation and casual use. Compared to PS VR2 / PC-tethered headsets PS VR2: excellent visuals and haptics but needs PS5 and is pure VR (no full-color passthrough MR in the same way). PC VR (HTC Vive, Index): often higher fidelity via powerful GPUs, but more complex setup and no standalone mode. Quest 3: sweet spot of mobility + MR + cost; it can also act as a wireless PC VR headset via Wi-Fi 6E. As a creative / dev tool Strong support for Unity and Unreal with official Meta XR SDKs, samples, and “building blocks” for hands, passthrough, spatial anchors, mesh APIs, etc. Runs completely untethered, so you can build: site-specific MR pieces in galleries, classrooms, outdoors (if safe); prototypes that don’t depend on a PC nearby. Very healthy store ecosystem: billions in Quest Store revenue overall → a real publishing channel for experimental games, apps, or tools. Summary Quest 3 (2023–2025) = mid-range, mass-market MR headset — Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, standalone, color passthrough, strong Unity/Unreal support, good enough optics, huge ecosystem. History (very condensed) Originated as a project by three Danish devs (David Helgason, Joachim Ante, Nicholas Francis) around 2002–2004 under the company Over the Edge Entertainment (OTEE) in Denmark. Unity 1.0 released June 2005 at Apple’s WWDC as a Mac-only game engine. Then expanded to Windows, web, consoles, and later mobile; became huge with iPhone (2007–2008) by making mobile 3D dev accessible. Today (2025): latest LTS line is Unity 6000.x LTS, still focused on cross-platform games, apps, and XR. What Unity is good at (esp. for creative tech & MR) Rapid prototyping & experimentation Short iteration loops, tons of tutorials, assets, templates. Great fit for “creative technologist wants to try a weird idea in a weekend”. Mobile + standalone XR Very mature Android / Quest toolchain; most Quest titles are built in Unity. Component-based design Easy to wire behaviours via components, C#, visual scripting, and to reuse “prefabs”. Ecosystem Asset Store, 3rd-party tools (generative art tools, VFX, shaders, etc.), integrations with sensors, MIDI, OSC, etc. For Meta Quest 3 specifically: Unity + Meta XR SDK gives you: prefabs for camera rigs, hands, interactions; APIs for passthrough, depth/meshing, spatial anchors; MR “building blocks” that let you stand up interactive prototypes fast. History (very condensed) Developed by Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney starting around 1995 for the game Unreal. Unreal Engine 1 powers Unreal (1998) and later Unreal Tournament, then gets licensed to other studios. UE2/UE3 dominate high-end PC/console shooters and action games in the 2000s. Unreal Engine 4 (2014) brings modern PBR graphics, Blueprints visual scripting, and a friendlier licensing model. Unreal Engine 5 (2021→) adds Nanite (virtualized geometry) and Lumen (global illumination), pushing near-cinematic real-time graphics; by 2025, UE5 is the reference for high-fidelity real-time 3D across games, film, and virtual production. What Unreal is good at (esp. for XR / MR) Visual fidelity / cinematic graphics Ideal when you want realistic lighting, massive scenes, film-like look. Virtual production & architecture Widely used in studios for LED volumes, previs, archviz, automotive demos. Blueprints Node-based scripting that lets artists/technical artists do complex logic without writing C++. For XR / Quest-style devices: Unreal has XR templates and plugins for Meta Quest, but historically has been more dominant in PC-tethered or high-end standalone content (Quest can run UE, but many devs prefer Unity there for speed & tooling). Strong choice if your creative goal is cinematic MR or very polished visuals, or if you’re already in the Unreal ecosystem (film, archviz, game studios). This is not about “better engine”, but different personalities: Feels like: fast sketchbook / lab for XR. Best for: rapid MR experiments, interactive installations, generative pieces; educational apps, playful prototypes, standing/room-scale toys. Pros: lighter editor, very mature Quest pipeline, huge community of Quest tutorials; Asset Store and Meta’s Building Blocks help you get MR + hands working quickly. Feels like: film set / high-end studio. Best for: visually ambitious MR experiences; projects that may also target PC/console, virtual production, or cinematic workflows. Pros: Unreal’s rendering + tools (Sequencer, Nanite, Lumen) are very powerful when visual polish is a priority. Unity: Lower friction to learn; great for workshops, quick experiments, interactive art. Strong combination with Quest 3 when the goal is exploring ideas (e.g., body-based interfaces, data-driven visuals in MR). Unreal: Stronger when the project demands cinema-level visuals or must integrate with film / broadcast pipelines. Good for teams where artists already live in Unreal (VFX/film). You can absolutely mix them in your practice: Prototype concepts, interaction, and MR behaviours in Unity + Quest 3. For selected pieces that need a “wow visual factor” or are tied to film/TV, port or rebuild in Unreal. FBX (Filmbox) is a file format developed by Autodesk. It is a multi-purpose container widely used to store 3D models, animations, textures, and even entire scenes. FBX is well supported in both Unreal Engine and Unity, and is often used as an “exchange format” between the two, even though there can be subtle differences depending on how the file was exported.What an FBX file can contain: Geometry (3D models) Animations (object or character motion) Textures and materials Lights and cameras Rigging and skeletons (for characters) Animation curves / paths (for characters, cameras, or objects) Unity can read FBX files natively, and they can be imported directly into your project. General workflow: Drag the FBX file into the Assets folder of your Unity project. Unity will automatically import the 3D model, animations, and textures (if they are embedded or correctly referenced). In the Inspector, you can adjust the FBX import settings (scale, rig, animation import, materials, etc.). If the FBX contains animations, you can set up animation controllers in Unity to drive those clips. Once imported, the FBX can be placed into the scene, and you can attach effects, scripts, or interactions on top of it.

mrl-glitch-test-the-avatars-animation-wi.title: MRL Glitch - Test the avatars animation with passthrough
mrl-glitch-test-the-avatars-animation-wi.description:
Summary
Before creating the project
After creating the project (the short path to Passthrough)
A) Switch to Android (Unity 6 = Build Profiles)
B) Enable XR (OpenXR) — and validate the build for Quest 3 (Unity 6)
B1) Enable OpenXR on Android
B2) Configure OpenXR (interaction profile + features)
B3) Confirm essential Player Settings (Android/Quest compatibility)
B4) Make sure nothing “Required” is still pending
C) Import and configure the Meta XR SDK (for Passthrough on Quest 3)
C1) Import Meta XR All-in-One SDK (the correct way on Unity 6)
C2) Run Meta XR Project Setup Tool (apply Recommended fixes and resolve anything required)
D) Add Passthrough to the scene
Headset test
E) Import FBX + autoplay loop + WorldRoot (world-anchored)
E1) Import the FBXs
E2) Set each FBX animation to loop
E3) (Important) Rig = Generic (to preserve transforms/scale from “transform baked”)
E4) Create a WorldRoot (world anchor reference)
E5) Put one FBX into the scene as a child of WorldRoot
E6) Autoplay — Animator Controller
E7) Quick sanity check in the Editor
F) Quest test (passthrough + FBX in the world)
F1) Fix: avatar “disappears” when you turn/move sideways (culling / bounds)
F2) (Best practice) Avoid “weird offset”: keep the FBX clean, fix axis on WorldRoot, offset on AnimOffset Start MRL Glitch ProjectOpen Meta Quest DeveloperHub<br>Confirm USB connectionUnity Hub → NewProject<br>Template: 3DURPA: Switch to Android<br>File →Build Profiles → AndroidB: Enable OpenXRB1: Enable OpenXR onAndroid<br>XR Plug-in ManagementB2: ConfigureOpenXR<br>Interaction Profiles +FeaturesB3: PlayerSettings<br>IL2CPP+ ARM64B4: ProjectValidation<br>ResolveRequired fixesC: Import Meta XR SDKC1: Package Manager<br>My Assets →Meta XR All-in-One SDKC2: Meta XR Project SetupTool<br>Apply All RecommendedfixesManuallyFixable ItemsData Use Checkup: IgnorePackage Name: com.xxx.xxxD: Add PassthroughBuilding Blocks:<br>CameraRig + PassthroughRemove/Disable Main CameraKeep Directional LightBuild And Run →Quest<br>Library → UnknownSourcesPassthrough<br>working?E: Import FBXDebug: review steps A-DE1: Place FBXs in Assets/FBX/E2: For each FBX:<br>Loop Time + LoopPoseE3: Rig = Generic<br>preservebaked transformsE4: CreateWorldRoot<br>EmptyGameObject 0,0,0E5: FBX as child ofWorldRoot<br>Transform 0,0,0E6: AnimatorController<br>Autoplay loopE7: Test Play in EditorF: Build And Run → QuestAvataranimating<br>+Passthrough?Avatardisappears<br>when moving?Debug: review step EF1: Fix Culling<br>SkinnedMesh Renderer:<br>UpdateWhen OffscreenF2: Adjust positioningFinal Structure:<br>WorldRootrotation -90,0,0<br>└─AnimOffset position 0,-2,0<br>└─ 01_Anim 0,0,0✅ Project Complete:<br>Passthrough + Animated FBXYesNoYesNoYesNo Open Meta Quest Developer Hub (MQDH) Confirm the Quest shows as connected (USB). If a prompt appears inside the headset (“Allow USB debugging?”), accept it. Unity Hub → New project Template: 3D (URP) (or “3D Core” if URP is not available; I prefer URP because it’s usually the most stable path with XR). Inside SRP there are two main pipelines: URP (Universal Render Pipeline) → lightweight, good for VR/MR/mobile (Quest fits here) HDRP (High Definition Render Pipeline) → heavy, aimed at high-end visuals (not what you want for Quest) Suggested name: MRLGlitch_Passthrough_FBX_Test Location: a short path without weird spaces (to avoid Android build headaches). There isn’t an “official Unity Hub template” that ships with passthrough ready. The real shortcut is: Create 3D URP + import Meta XR SDK + run the Project Setup Tool + add Passthrough Building Blocks. Go to File → Build Profiles On the left panel, select Android Click Switch Platform (or Switch / Activate, depending on what appears) Wait for Unity to finish switching (asset reimport may happen) Go to Edit → Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management Select the Android tab Check OpenXR Still in Project Settings, open OpenXR (menu on the left column) Under Enabled Interaction Profiles, ensure at least 1 profile is enabled Example: Meta Quest Touch Pro Controller Profile (or equivalent) Under OpenXR Feature Groups, make sure the Meta XR group is enabled/selected (when available) Go to Edit → Project Settings → Player Tab Android Open Other Settings and confirm: Scripting Backend = IL2CPP Target Architectures: ARM64 checked (ARMv7 unchecked, if it appears) (if requested by validation) Minimum API Level / Target API Level: keep what Unity/OpenXR suggests Go to Edit → Project Settings → Project Validation Confirm there are no Required fix (red) items related to OpenXR/Android Note: if you see “Required fixes” in the status bar referencing Project Setup Tool, that’s usually from Meta XR (step C), not from OpenXR. Open Window → Package Manager In the top-left of Package Manager, change the Source to My Assets (not “Unity Registry” — you won’t find Meta’s SDK there) Search for Meta XR All-in-One SDK Click Download (if it isn’t downloaded yet) Click Import In the import window, keep the defaults and confirm Import If Meta XR All-in-One SDK doesn’t show up under My Assets: It means the asset hasn’t been added to your Unity/Asset Store account yet. The correct action is to add it to your account, and then it will appear under “My Assets” in Unity. Open the Meta XR Tools panel: Top menu: Meta → Meta XR Tools (or click “Welcome to Meta XR SDK” if it already opened) Click Project Setup Tool On the Project Setup Tool screen: Check the status at the top. In your case it looks like: “There are X outstanding Recommended fixes.” Under Recommended Items, click Apply All Under Manually Fixable Items, handle like this (for a passthrough + FBX local test): Complete a Data Use Checkup… For local testing (not store release), you can ignore. If the tool allows it, use Mark as Fixed just to clear the warning. Set up the application ID and the package name… Package name: worth setting now to avoid build confusion on the Quest. Example: com.cieglitch.mrlglitch.passthroughtest Application ID (Meta Platform / entitlement): if you are not using Platform SDK now, you can ignore (or “Mark as Fixed” if allowed) (Optional, but useful) If the Console shows something like: “at least the Oculus Touch Interaction Profile should be included…” that’s from OpenXR (not the Meta Setup Tool). Fix it here: Edit → Project Settings → OpenXR Under Enabled Interaction Profiles, also add Oculus Touch Controller Interaction Profile (or equivalent) Expected result: after Apply All, warnings drop a lot and the project is in a Quest-friendly configuration (performance + compatibility). Open Meta XR Tools Click Building Blocks Add the minimum blocks: Camera Rig (or the equivalent Meta rig/camera block) Passthrough Make sure you don’t have two cameras: If your scene still has the default URP Main Camera, either: disable it (GameObject checkbox), or delete it The Meta rig will provide the camera XR needs. Ensure your 3D content can be visible over passthrough: Keep a Directional Light (or a simple light) in the scene — without light, FBX meshes can look dark/invisible even if passthrough works. File → Build Profiles → Android → Build And Run macOS will open a Build Android window asking where to save the APK. In Save As: type something like MRLGlitch_Passthrough_Test.apk Save outside the project folder, e.g. a “Builds” folder Click Save If Unity warns: “Android SDK is missing required platform API level(s): 32” click Update Android SDK to install Android SDK Platform 32 (this is a SDK component and usually only needs to be installed once per machine). After the build finishes and the APK is installed: On Quest: Library → Unknown Sources → open your app You should see the real world (passthrough) + your Unity scene on top. Put the files in Assets/FBX/ (e.g. 01_Anim.fbx ... 05_Anim.fbx) For each FBX (01_Anim.fbx, 02_Anim.fbx, etc.): Click the FBX in the Project (Assets) In the Inspector: Animation tab Check Import Animations (if unchecked) In Clips (or the listed clip), enable: Loop Time (optional) Loop Pose Click Apply Since the FBXs came with transform baked (Unreal → Unity pipeline), it’s safer to keep the rig as Generic. In the Project, select the asset 01_Anim.fbx (not 01_Anim in the Hierarchy) In the Inspector, open the Rig tab Set Animation Type to Generic Click Apply If you select the object in the Hierarchy, you won’t see Model/Rig/Animation tabs — those tabs only appear when selecting the FBX file in the Project. In the Hierarchy: GameObject → Create Empty Rename it to: WorldRoot With WorldRoot selected, in Inspector → Transform: Position: X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 0 Rotation: 0, 0, 0 Scale: 1, 1, 1 This keeps content “fixed in the world” (not attached to the camera). In a first test, it’s anchored to the reference frame created when the app starts. Drag 01_Anim.fbx from Project into the Hierarchy Drag it to become a child of WorldRoot (indented under it) Keep the FBX Transform clean (local to WorldRoot): Position: 0,0,0 Rotation: 0,0,0 Scale: 1,1,1 If pressing Play does not make the FBX animate automatically: In Project: Assets → Create → Animator Controller Name: AC_01_Anim Double click the controller to open the Animator window Expand the FBX asset (small arrow next to the file) and find the Animation Clip Drag the clip into the Animator window Ensure it becomes the Default State (orange) Select the FBX GameObject in the Hierarchy and in Inspector: Add an Animator component (if it doesn’t exist) In Controller, assign AC_01_Anim ✅ Result: when the app starts, the animation plays automatically and (because of Loop Time) loops. Press Play Confirm: the FBX is visible the animation runs in a loop File → Build Profiles → Android → Build And Run On Quest: Library → Unknown Sources → open the app You should see: passthrough the avatar animating in loop, fixed in the world Symptom: the avatar disappears when you move right/left, like there’s a viewing limit.Common cause: Unity culls skinned meshes based on the Skinned Mesh Renderer bounds. Some animated FBXs import bounds that are too small/wrong.✅ Fix (worked in our case): In the Hierarchy, expand 01_Anim (arrow ▶) and select the child that contains the mesh (e.g. Body, Mesh, etc.) In the Inspector, find Skinned Mesh Renderer Enable: ✅ Update When Offscreen Note: this component usually is NOT on the 01_Anim root (root often has only Transform + Animator). You must click a child that holds the mesh. Keep 01_Anim with a clean local Transform: Position 0,0,0 Rotation 0,0,0 Scale 1,1,1 Use WorldRoot only for axis/orientation correction: Rotation X = -90 (axis fix, if needed) Create a child under WorldRoot named AnimOffset, and use it to place the avatar in space: Adjust AnimOffset.Position (example: Y = -2 in your case) Why did Y = -2 work (instead of pushing on Z)? With WorldRoot.X = -90, the local axes effectively rotate, so “moving on Y” at the AnimOffset level can behave like “moving forward/back” in world space (depending on your axis fix + imported rig orientation).

headers.heading: Summary
Before creating the project
After creating the project (the short path to Passthrough)
A) Switch to Android (Unity 6 = Build Profiles)
B) Enable XR (OpenXR) — and validate the build for Quest 3 (Unity 6)
B1) Enable OpenXR on Android
B2) Configure OpenXR (interaction profile + features)
B3) Confirm essential Player Settings (Android/Quest compatibility)
B4) Make sure nothing “Required” is still pending
C) Import and configure the Meta XR SDK (for Passthrough on Quest 3)
C1) Import Meta XR All-in-One SDK (the correct way on Unity 6)
C2) Run Meta XR Project Setup Tool (apply Recommended fixes and resolve anything required)
D) Add Passthrough to the scene
Headset test
E) Import FBX + autoplay loop + WorldRoot (world-anchored)
E1) Import the FBXs
E2) Set each FBX animation to loop
E3) (Important) Rig = Generic (to preserve transforms/scale from “transform baked”)
E4) Create a WorldRoot (world anchor reference)
E5) Put one FBX into the scene as a child of WorldRoot
E6) Autoplay — Animator Controller
E7) Quick sanity check in the Editor
F) Quest test (passthrough + FBX in the world)
F1) Fix: avatar “disappears” when you turn/move sideways (culling / bounds)
F2) (Best practice) Avoid “weird offset”: keep the FBX clean, fix axis on WorldRoot, offset on AnimOffset

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
